title: Checkpoint: Civil War and Reconstruction
objective: After this level you can explain how the war ended slavery and what Reconstruction promised, won and lost.
summary: From Dred Scott to 1877 on one timeline: a war that ended slavery, amendments that promised citizenship and the vote, and a retreat that left those promises unprotected.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: freedom was won in war. Equality was promised, then abandoned.
cards.body: Twenty years, from a court ruling to a troop withdrawal. Let’s put the whole story on one line.

cards.headline: Civil War and Reconstruction, in order

events.label: Dred Scott: Black Americans declared not citizens
Lee surrenders; the 13th Amendment ends slavery
The last federal troops leave the South

cards.headline: Won, then lost
cards.body: Between 1865 and 1877, the United States abolished slavery and wrote citizenship and voting rights into the Constitution, then withdrew the federal troops that protected them. The gains were real: Freedmen’s Bureau schools, and Black lawmakers like Hiram Revels in Congress. So was the backlash, from Klan terror to the bargain of 1877. The war settled slavery for good. Reconstruction’s promises stayed in the Constitution, waiting for later generations to enforce them.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: How the fight over slavery split the Union, and how the war became a war to end slavery.
Why Lincoln framed emancipation as a war measure, and what the Proclamation left out.
How enslaved people and Black soldiers helped win their own freedom.
What the three amendments promised, and why those promises went unprotected after 1877.

questions.prompt: Put these events of the Civil War and Reconstruction in order, from earliest to latest.
items: The last federal troops leave the South
questions.explanation: Dred Scott came in 1857, Fort Sumter in 1861, the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863, Lee’s surrender in 1865, the 14th Amendment in 1868, and the last federal troops left the South in 1877.

questions.prompt: Vicksburg’s surrender in July 1863 gave the Union _____.

options.label: the Confederate capital
options.rationale: Richmond was in Virginia, far to the east.

questions.explanation: Vicksburg’s fall gave the Union the Mississippi and split the Confederacy.

questions.prompt: Why can Reconstruction be described as rights won, then lost?

options.label: Congress repealed the Reconstruction amendments once federal troops left in 1877
options.rationale: The amendments stayed in the Constitution.

options.label: Slavery returned after federal troops left
options.rationale: The war settled slavery for good.

options.label: The Constitution promised rights, but federal protection of them was withdrawn
The Supreme Court ended the 13th Amendment

questions.explanation: The amendments stayed, but after 1877 the troops that protected Southern Republican governments were gone.

questions.prompt: What did the Emancipation Proclamation announce about Black men and the military?

options.label: They would be drafted into the Confederate army and navy
They could join only as unpaid laborers
options.rationale: It accepted them into the Army and Navy.

options.label: They were barred from all military service
They would be accepted into the Union Army and Navy

questions.explanation: The Proclamation announced that Black men would be accepted into the Union Army and Navy.

questions.prompt: John Brown hoped enslaved people would rise up in 1859. How did many enslaved people actually seize freedom during the war?

options.label: By joining John Brown’s raid on Harpers Ferry
options.rationale: The raid failed in 1859, before the war.

options.label: By escaping to Union lines, as at Fort Monroe
By voting in the 1860 election
options.rationale: Enslaved people could not vote in 1860.

options.label: By moving to the Confederate capital

questions.explanation: From Fort Monroe onward, enslaved people escaped to Union lines, becoming “contraband of war.”
